name: Vector (linear algebra)
definition: An ordered list of numbers treated as one object: a point, a direction, or data. Vectors add component-wise and scale by multiplying every component.

examples.explanation: A three-component vector.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Matrix
definition: A rectangular array of numbers that acts on vectors by matrix multiplication. Matrices compose linear transformations: applying B then A is the product AB.

examples.explanation: A two-by-two matrix with rows (1,2) and (3,4).

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Matrix transpose
definition: Flips a matrix across its diagonal: rows become columns. The entry in row i, column j of Aᵀ is the entry in row j, column i of A.

examples.explanation: Rows and columns exchange places.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Matrix inverse
definition: The matrix that undoes A: AA⁻¹ = A⁻¹A = I. Only square matrices with nonzero determinant have one; others are singular.

examples.explanation: Solving a linear system by inverting A.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Determinant
definition: A single number measuring how a matrix scales volume: zero means the transformation flattens space (no inverse), and the sign records orientation flips.

examples.tex: \det\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix} = ad - bc
examples.explanation: The two-by-two determinant formula.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Matrix trace
definition: Sums the diagonal entries of a square matrix. The trace equals the sum of the eigenvalues and is unchanged by cyclic reorderings of products.

examples.explanation: One plus four.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Matrix rank
definition: Counts the independent rows (equivalently, columns) of a matrix: the dimension of its image. Full rank means no redundancy; rank deficiency means some rows repeat information.

examples.explanation: The second row is twice the first, so one direction survives.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Eigenvalue
definition: A scalar λ for which Av = λv for some nonzero vector v: the transformation stretches v by λ without changing its direction. Eigenvalues reveal stability, vibration modes and principal directions.

examples.explanation: The characteristic equation whose roots are the eigenvalues.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Eigenvector
definition: A nonzero vector a transformation only stretches: Av = λv. The direction is preserved while the eigenvalue λ sets the scale (possibly flipping or collapsing it).

examples.explanation: (1,0) is stretched by 2 along the x-axis.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Inner product
definition: Generalizes the dot product: a scalar measuring alignment of two vectors. Zero means orthogonal. Lengths, angles and projections all derive from it.
reading: “the inner product of u and v”.

examples.explanation: The axes are perpendicular.

contexts.meaning: The dot product: sum of component-wise products.
Often an integral of the product over a domain.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Dot product
definition: The Euclidean inner product: multiply matching components and add. It equals |u||v|cos θ, linking algebra to the angle between vectors.

examples.explanation: One times three plus two times four.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Cross product
definition: Produces a vector perpendicular to two 3D vectors, with length equal to the parallelogram area they span. Direction follows the right-hand rule; order matters (u × v = −v × u).

examples.explanation: x cross y gives z.

commonMistakes: Treating × as ordinary multiplication; the result is a vector, not a scalar.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Kronecker delta
definition: Equals 1 when its indices match and 0 otherwise. It writes the identity matrix compactly and sifts sums to a single term.

examples.explanation: Only the j = i term survives the sum.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Identity matrix
definition: The matrix with ones on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere. Multiplying by I leaves any compatible matrix or vector unchanged.

examples.explanation: The two-by-two identity.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Permutation
definition: Counts ordered selections of k objects from n: n!/(n−k)!. Order matters here, which distinguishes permutations from combinations.
reading: “P of n k” or “permutations of n taken k at a time”.

examples.explanation: Twenty ordered pairs from five objects.

name: Combination
definition: Counts unordered selections of k objects from n, equal to the binomial coefficient. Same count as C(n,k); the C-notation is common in probability texts.
reading: “C of n k” or “n choose k”.

examples.explanation: Ten unordered pairs from five objects.

sources.label: OpenStax Precalculus 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Graph (vertices and edges)
definition: A graph G pairs a vertex set V with an edge set E of vertex pairs. Paths, cycles and trees are all special graphs; edges may carry direction or weights.
reading: “G equals V E: vertices and edges”.

examples.explanation: Two vertices joined by one edge.

sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Modular arithmetic
definition: Arithmetic on remainders after division by n: numbers differing by a multiple of n are treated as equal. Powers, sums and products all reduce mod n.

examples.explanation: Seventeen leaves remainder 2 on division by 5.
Add, then keep the remainder.

name: Floor and ceiling
definition: Floor rounds down to the nearest integer at or below x; ceiling rounds up to the nearest integer at or above x. Brackets point down for floor, up for ceiling.

examples.explanation: Round down to 3.
Round up to 4.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Linear span
definition: All vectors obtainable by combining the given ones with scalar weights. A set of vectors spans a space when every vector there is such a combination.

examples.explanation: Weighted combinations a·(1,0) + b·(0,1) reach every point (a, b).

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Kernel (null space)
definition: All inputs a linear map sends to zero. Its dimension (the nullity) plus the rank equals the number of columns: the rank–nullity theorem.

examples.explanation: Both rows dot (−2, 1) to zero: −2 + 2 = 0.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Orthogonal matrix
definition: A square matrix with orthonormal columns: QᵀQ = I, so Q⁻¹ = Qᵀ and lengths and angles are preserved. Rotations and reflections are the geometric examples.

examples.explanation: The rotation columns are unit vectors at right angles, so the product is the identity.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Generating function
definition: Encodes a whole sequence as the coefficients of a power series: G(x) = a₀ + a₁x + a₂x² + …. Recurrences become algebra on G, and extracting coefficients solves counting problems.

examples.explanation: For F₀ = 0, F₁ = 1: expanding gives x + x² + 2x³ + 3x⁴ + 5x⁵, the Fibonacci numbers.

sources.license: Author/university course notes; consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Pigeonhole principle
definition: Putting more items than containers forces sharing: with m+1 items in m boxes, some box holds at least two. Simple to state, surprisingly powerful for existence proofs.

examples.explanation: Thirteen people and twelve months force two into one month.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Binomial theorem
aliases: a plus b to the n
definition: Expands powers of a sum with binomial coefficients: (a+b)ⁿ = Σ C(n,k) aⁿ⁻ᵏbᵏ. Each term chooses which factors contribute b.

examples.explanation: Coefficients 1, 2, 1 count the ways to choose zero, one, or two ones.

sources.label: OpenStax Precalculus 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Basis and dimension
definition: A basis is a minimal spanning set: independent vectors from which every vector is uniquely combined. Its size is the dimension, an invariant of the space, not of the choice.

examples.explanation: The three unit vectors e₁, e₂, e₃ form one basis; every basis has three vectors.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Linear independence
definition: Vectors are independent when only the all-zero combination gives zero: none is redundant. A dependent set contains a vector already spanned by the rest.

examples.explanation: Nonzero solutions exist (e.g. c₁ = 2, c₂ = −1), so the pair is dependent.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Diagonalization
definition: Writing A = PDP⁻¹ with D diagonal: in the eigenvector basis, the map is pure scaling. Possible exactly when eigenvectors span the space; distinct eigenvalues always suffice.

examples.explanation: Already diagonal: eigenvalues 2 and 3 act along the axes.
